newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA issues stopgap air toxics rule.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA issues stopgap air toxics rule.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency issued a rule allowing manufacturers to rebuild or expand existing plants without new pollution controls as long as they do not increase emissions by more than 10 tons a year for any single toxic air pollutant or by 25 tons a year for all toxic air pollutants, an EPA spokesman said Monday.
The rule was designed as a stopgap measure to give the EPA time to regulate all 174 industries nationwide under the Clean Air Act. Since 1990, it has issued rules for 47 industries.
The final rule was less stringent than an initial proposal which manufacturers battled over the last two years.

Under its initial proposal, EPA wanted to set different caps on increases in emissions, ranging from about one to 10 tons a year, depending on the pollutant to be regulated. The limit for dioxin, for example, would have been tighter than for benzene.
Industries such as semiconductor manufacturers that have to retool rapidly to react to market shifts did not want to have to apply to EPA every time they made minor plant changes.
Under pressure from industry and states, EPA simplified the final rule by setting one threshold for all air toxics.
EPA estimated that at least 50 and possibly as many as 400 facilities a year would be subject to new pollution controls under the rule from 1997 through 2003.
Complying with the rule would cost industry around $4 million a year, the EPA spokesman said.
